items.title: Redesign how your team ships software with AI agents
items.summary: AI agents are sending more and more code into review queues built for human-paced work. A coding assistant can speed up code writing, but it can’t show you whether review, security checks, and release approvals can keep pace with all that extra code. AI-native engineering — the practice of intentionally designing the engineering process so people and agents each do what they are best suited to — starts with identifying delivery bottlenecks, then deciding how much autonomy agents should have and how to maintain control as you scale.The AI-Native Engineering Playbook, launching this week, helps teams turn faster coding into faster delivery by redesigning how they ship software with agents. Every practice in the playbook is grounded in insights from engineering leaders at GitLab, our customers, and members of our Software Engineering Leadership Forum (SELF) community. We also partnered with IT Revolution to incorporate findings from a diverse group of practitioners looking at AI-native software development from a number of different angles, from code review to agent autonomy.Below are a few of the questions we sought to answer in the process of creating the playbook.Where does the bottleneck go when coding gets faster?Coding used to be the slowest, most expensive part of building software. Agents removed the bottleneck on coding, and the constraint moved to everything around the code: waiting for clarifications, environments, approvals, and other teams. GitLab’s AI Accountability Report, based on an April 2026 survey of 1,528 DevSecOps professionals, found that 79% of respondents agreed that individual developer productivity has improved with AI, but the overall software delivery process has not accelerated at the same pace.Large enterprises typically have software delivery lead times of well over 200 days, with active development taking only 10% to 20% of that time. The numbers explain why a faster coding step is often disappointing in the long run. For example, imagine a 281-day delivery cycle that involves about 32 days spent on coding. Make coding 50% faster, and you save about 16 days, a 6% improvement. But if you take coding all the way to zero, around 88% of the lead time stays untouched. [1]GitLab’s research similarly found that DevSecOps professionals reported spending only 16% of their time writing new code, and 85% agreed AI has shifted the bottleneck from writing code to reviewing and validating it.That means your first job is diagnosis. Take one small, real change and trace it from request to production, marking every wait and every handoff. The longest waits show where your next improvement is, and it's rarely in the code. Watch where an agent stalls on a small task, too. The stall usually points to a standard nobody documented, an environment that’s hard to start, or context that lived in a single person’s head.How much autonomy should agents have?Agent autonomy should depend on how well you can verify the agent output. Imagine a ladder with four stages, ranging from semi-manual (a person approving every step) to fully autonomous (a zero-touch workflow). In this framework, there are clear rules for advancing up the ladder: no rungs can be skipped, and each step up needs to be backed with evidence from the rung below. [2]Stage 1: Humans are in the loop at every stepStage 2: Humans are still in the loop, but the agent executes within set boundsStage 3: Humans are out of the loop for normal operation and handle only exceptionsStage 4: A zero-touch workflow, where the agent manages itself end to end, calling in a human only when predefined thresholds are met [2]It’s also important for a named human to stay accountable for every AI-enabled workflow, and the line between a human reviewing and a human monitoring should be explicitly defined, since loose or arbitrary definitions tend to erode under time pressure. [3]That erosion is the trap. A person who is nominally in the loop but approves everything gives the appearance of control without the benefits, and habit and volume can easily turn review into mindless rubber-stamping. A checkpoint nobody actually exercises is worse than none, because it creates confidence where the system needs scrutiny.The way up is to earn each step on evidence. Set an explicit accuracy or success threshold before you widen a step, then move people from reviewing each step to monitoring the whole. An agent that stops more often to ask for help is a healthy sign, since the system is refusing to outrun its own evidence. [2]How do you review code at agent volume?Widening autonomy depends on catching mistakes, and that puts pressure on code review. Review at merge time was built for human-paced output. Agents raise the rate of change, and manual review of every change set has become unsustainable.
